newsitem.title: UK: London gold steadies to fix just above morning.
newsitem.headline: London gold steadies to fix just above morning.

text.p: Precious metals prices continued along narrowly mixed lines on Tuesday afternoon reflecting a relatively quiet opening in New York, dealers said.
Earlier the gold market crept above $344.00 per ounce on short covering which came in after a floor around $343.50 held mid-morning.

A ruling from the European Union (EU) on how the central banks could use revenue from gold sales stimulated the market only briefly. The price bucked up by about a dollar but quickly gave back the gain.

"It's confusing. I don't know how much of it has to do with news on central bank sales because there was a little shortcovering coming in just then and it may have exaggerated the move," one dealer said.
Gold was fixed at $344.30 per ounce compared with $343.75 this morning and $345.50 on Friday.
At the fixing the Comex April contract was showing a $0.60 gain at $346.60 in what dealers said was a pretty quiet start to the session.

Eurostat the EU's statistical office ruled that gold sales by national central banks could not be used to reduce budget deficits in line with Maastricht Treaty criteria on membership of Economic and Monetary Union.
But the ruling did not suggest that outstanding public debt could not be reduced through the use of gold sales.

"The news is that central banks can't just sell gold and do a little book fiddle to fit the budget criteria. But there's nothing to stop European banks selling gold for any other reason," one dealer said.
Last month the Dutch central bank announced it had sold 300 tonnes of gold from its reserves.
Gold prices slumped late last week partly on rumours that another European central bank had followed the Dutch bank's example.
"It's a serious statement and must be treated seriously. But it doesn't actually change the status quo, with the likelihood of central banks selling reserves one bit," a dealer said.
A continuing strong dollar kept the gold price under pressure but dealers said its relatively low level appeared to be stimulating good physical buying in the Middle East.
Silver stuck around $4.86/$4.88, down four cents from Friday while platinum and palladium were little changed at $349.50/$350.50 and $123.50/$124.50 respectively.
